lessonTitle: Drag on Bodies: Skin Friction, Form Drag and Streamlining

blocks.text: A 25 mm steel cable on a suspension tower hums in a steady gale, and the wind load on the whole span is dominated by one number: the drag coefficient of a cylinder. If the same cable were wrapped in a teardrop-shaped fairing of the same height, the load would drop by an order of magnitude even though the frontal width is unchanged. This unit explains why.

blocks.markdown: A body in a stream feels a force from the fluid. The component parallel to the free-stream velocity is the **drag**, and it has two physical origins. **Skin friction** (viscous shear drag) comes from the shear stress $\tau_w$ acting tangentially on the surface. **Pressure drag** (form drag) comes from the pressure distribution acting normal to the surface: when the flow separates, the pressure behind the body stays low, and the net pressure force on the front exceeds that on the back. The sum is the total drag.

blocks.title: Drag coefficient
blocks.text: The drag force $D$ (N) on a body is written $D=C_D\,\tfrac12\rho U^2 A$, where $\rho$ is fluid density (kg/m$^3$), $U$ is the approach speed (m/s), $A$ is a reference area (m$^2$) and $C_D$ is the dimensionless drag coefficient. For bluff bodies such as spheres and cylinders, $A$ is the frontal (projected) area; for flat plates and streamlined bodies it may be the wetted or plan area, so always check which area a quoted $C_D$ refers to.

blocks.latex: D=C_D\,\tfrac12\rho U^2A,\qquad A_{sphere}=\frac{\pi d^2}{4},\quad A_{cylinder}=d\,L,\qquad Re=\frac{\rho U d}{\mu}
blocks.caption: Drag law with frontal areas and Reynolds number based on diameter

blocks.markdown: $C_D$ depends on shape and on Reynolds number. Typical chart values for smooth bodies in the range $10^3\lesssim Re\lesssim2\times10^5$ are about 0.47 for a sphere and about 1.2 for a long circular cylinder (cross-flow). At much lower $Re<1$ (creeping flow) Stokes' law gives $C_D=24/Re$ for a sphere. At around $Re\approx3\times10^5$ the boundary layer on a sphere or cylinder becomes turbulent, separation moves downstream, the wake narrows and $C_D$ drops suddenly (the **drag crisis**). All numbers in this unit are representative values from charts, not exact.

blocks.title: Drag on a ball in air
blocks.prompt: A smooth sphere of diameter 0.12 m moves through still air at 20 m/s. Use typical air properties (density 1.20 kg/m^3, viscosity 1.8e-5 Pa s) and the chart value C_D = 0.47 appropriate to this range. Find the drag force.

steps.text: Compute the Reynolds number to check that the chart value applies (the chart plateau is about 1e3 to 2e5).
Dynamic pressure 0.5 rho U^2 = 0.5(1.20)(20^2) = 240 Pa, then apply the drag law.

blocks.answer: Re = 1.60e+05 (inside the plateau range), D = 1.28 N.

rows: Thin flat plate parallel to flow
blocks.caption: Typical drag coefficients; the values are representative, not design data

blocks.title: Wind load on a cable
blocks.prompt: A smooth circular cable of diameter 25 mm and length 8.0 m is perpendicular to a steady 12 m/s wind. With air density 1.20 kg/m^3, viscosity 1.8e-5 Pa s and chart value C_D = 1.2 for this range, estimate the drag force on the cable.

steps.text: Check the Reynolds number to confirm the chart value of about 1.2 is appropriate (1e3 to 2e5).
The reference area for a cylinder in cross-flow is diameter times length.
Dynamic pressure 0.5(1.20)(12^2) = 86.4 Pa, so the drag is C_D times this times the area.

blocks.markdown: **Why does streamlining work?** On a bluff body the boundary layer meets an adverse pressure gradient on the rear half and separates, leaving a wide, low-pressure wake. The pressure on the back is then much lower than at the front, giving a large pressure drag. A long tapering tail makes the pressure rise gradual, so the boundary layer stays attached much further back and the wake is thin. The pressure on the rear surface then nearly recovers to its value at the front, and the pressure drag falls sharply. The price is a larger wetted area, hence more skin friction, so streamlining pays only when the form drag was the dominant term.

items: Identify the body and its reference area, and use the area the quoted $C_D$ is based on.
Compute $Re$ to see which part of the $C_D$ chart is relevant.
Read a typical $C_D$ and calculate the dynamic pressure $\tfrac12\rho U^2$ in pascals.
Multiply $D=C_D\cdot\tfrac12\rho U^2\cdot A$ and sanity-check the order of magnitude.
Ask whether skin friction or form drag dominates, and whether a streamlined shape would help.

blocks.title: Drag scales with the square of speed
blocks.text: At a fixed $C_D$, doubling the speed multiplies the drag by four and the power needed to overcome it ($P=DU$) by eight. This is why a small drop in $C_D$, achieved by fairings or smooth shapes, saves large amounts of energy on fast vehicles.

blocks.title: Do not mix areas
blocks.text: Quoting $C_D=0.47$ for a sphere and then using the surface area $4\pi r^2$ instead of the frontal area $\pi r^2$ gives an answer four times too large. Also remember that $C_D$ is not constant: near $Re\approx3\times10^5$ it can fall by a factor of about five (the drag crisis).

points: Total drag is skin friction plus pressure (form) drag; slender bodies are dominated by skin friction, bluff bodies by form drag.
$D=C_D\tfrac12\rho U^2A$ with the correct reference area; typical $C_D$ is about 0.47 for a sphere and 1.2 for a cylinder at moderate $Re$.
Streamlining delays separation and shrinks the wake, which lowers the pressure drag at the cost of some extra skin friction.
Drag grows with $U^2$ and the power to overcome it with $U^3$.

questions.stem: Which body in a high Reynolds number air stream has a drag that is dominated by skin friction rather than pressure (form) drag?

options.text: A flat disc facing the flow
A sphere in the range 1000 < Re < 200000
A thin flat plate aligned with the flow
A circular cylinder with its axis across the flow

questions.correctOptionText: A thin flat plate aligned with the flow

distractorRationale.a: A disc normal to the flow has almost entirely pressure drag.
distractorRationale.b: A sphere separates in this range, so form drag is by far the larger part.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: with the plate edge-on there is almost no frontal area and no pressure difference, so shear dominates.
distractorRationale.d: A cylinder in cross-flow separates and has a wide wake, so form drag dominates.

questions.explanation: A thin plate parallel to the flow presents almost no frontal area, so the pressure forces on its faces are normal to the flow direction and contribute almost nothing to drag; the viscous shear along the surface provides almost all of it. The other bodies are bluff and separate, with wide low-pressure wakes.

questions.stem: For a bluff body such as a sphere or a circular cylinder at Reynolds numbers around 10^4, most of the drag is due to the pressure distribution rather than to skin friction.
questions.explanation: Flow separates from a bluff body and leaves a wide wake of low pressure behind it, so the net pressure force on the body is large. The viscous shear force acting along the surface is only a few per cent of the total at these Reynolds numbers.

questions.stem: A smooth steel sphere of diameter 50 mm is towed through still water at a steady 0.80 m/s. Use water density 998 kg/m^3, and a typical chart drag coefficient of 0.47 (the Reynolds number is about 4e4, in the range where this value applies). Calculate the drag force in newtons.
questions.explanation: The frontal area is pi(0.05)^2/4 = 0.00196 m^2 and the dynamic pressure is 0.5(998)(0.80^2) = 319.4 Pa. Then D = 0.47 x 319.4 x 0.00196 = 0.295 N.

questions.stem: A long circular pile of diameter 40 mm stands in a steady river current of 1.5 m/s flowing perpendicular to the pile. Use water density 998 kg/m^3 and a typical drag coefficient of 1.2. Find the drag force per metre of pile length in N/m.
questions.explanation: The reference area per metre is d x 1 m = 0.040 m^2. The dynamic pressure is 0.5(998)(1.5^2) = 1122.8 Pa, so F/L = 1.2 x 1122.8 x 0.040 = 53.9 N/m.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how streamlining a bluff body (for example adding a long tapering tail) reduces its drag?

options.text: It increases the frontal area so the drag coefficient falls
It delays boundary layer separation, giving a narrower wake and a smaller pressure difference between front and rear
It removes skin friction completely by making the surface smooth
It makes the flow irrotational and so removes viscous effects everywhere

questions.correctOptionText: It delays boundary layer separation, giving a narrower wake and a smaller pressure difference between front and rear

distractorRationale.a: Larger frontal area would increase, not decrease, the drag for the same C_D.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a gradual pressure recovery keeps the flow attached and shrinks the low-pressure wake.
distractorRationale.c: Streamlining actually adds wetted area, so skin friction rises slightly; the saving comes from the pressure drag.
distractorRationale.d: The flow near the body is still viscous and the boundary layer is still present.

questions.explanation: The tail makes the adverse pressure gradient on the rear surface gentle, so the boundary layer stays attached to a much greater distance along the body. The wake is then thin, the rear pressure recovers close to the front value, and the pressure drag falls far more than skin friction rises.

questions.stem: A smooth sphere of diameter 0.30 m moves through air (typical density 1.20 kg/m^3) with a drag coefficient of 0.47 and experiences a drag force of 15 N. Find its speed in m/s.
questions.explanation: Rearranging D = C_D (0.5 rho U^2) A gives U = sqrt(2D/(rho C_D A)). With A = pi(0.30)^2/4 = 0.0707 m^2, U = sqrt(30/(1.20 x 0.47 x 0.0707)) = 27.4 m/s.

questions.stem: A body has a constant drag coefficient. If the approach speed is doubled, by what factor does the drag force change?

distractorRationale.a: This assumes drag is linear in speed, which only applies in creeping (Stokes) flow.
distractorRationale.b: This is the factor for the power needed, which scales as U^3, not for the force.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: drag is proportional to U^2.
distractorRationale.d: This would require D proportional to U^4.

questions.explanation: The drag law $D=C_D\tfrac12\rho U^2A$ is quadratic in speed, so doubling U gives four times the drag. The power $P=DU$ rises by a factor of eight.

questions.stem: Which pairing of body and dominant drag mechanism is correct for flow at high Reynolds number?

options.text: A parked lorry facing the wind: mainly skin friction
A long thin aerofoil at zero incidence: mainly skin friction
A flat plate normal to the flow: mainly skin friction
A circular cylinder in cross-flow: mainly skin friction

questions.correctOptionText: A long thin aerofoil at zero incidence: mainly skin friction

distractorRationale.a: A lorry is a bluff body with a large wake, so form drag dominates.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a slender, attached-flow body has small pressure drag.
distractorRationale.c: A plate facing the flow experiences almost entirely pressure drag.
distractorRationale.d: A cylinder across the flow separates, giving mostly form drag.

questions.explanation: A slender aerofoil at zero incidence has attached flow and small pressure drag, so friction on its wetted surface is the main contribution. Bluff bodies (plate normal to the flow, cylinder, lorry) have separated wakes and drag that is mostly pressure drag.

questions.stem: Distinguish skin friction drag from form (pressure) drag. Give one example of a body dominated by each, and explain physically why separation raises the form drag of a bluff body.
markingGuide: Skin friction drag: integral of wall shear stress component along the flow direction
Form drag: integral of the pressure component in the flow direction, caused by unequal front and rear pressure
Example dominated by skin friction: flat plate parallel to flow or thin aerofoil/streamlined body
Example dominated by form drag: sphere, cylinder, flat plate normal to flow or bluff vehicle
Separation occurs on the rear surface under adverse pressure gradient, leaving a wake at nearly constant low pressure, so rear surface pressure does not recover and net pressure force opposes motion
questions.explanation: The two contributions come from different surface integrals: shear stress tangential to the surface and pressure normal to it. When flow separates on a bluff body, the pressure behind the body stays low rather than rising back to its front value, so the pressure force dominates the drag.

questions.stem: A teardrop-shaped body and a sphere have the same frontal area of 0.020 m^2 and move through air (density 1.20 kg/m^3) at 30 m/s. Taking typical drag coefficients of 0.47 (sphere) and 0.06 (streamlined, based on frontal area), calculate the drag on each and explain, in terms of flow separation, why the values differ so much.
markingGuide: Streamlined drag = 0.06 x 540 x 0.020 = 0.65 N (ratio about 7.8)
Sphere: boundary layer separates near the equator, wide low-pressure wake, large pressure drag
Teardrop: gradual taper, delayed or no separation, narrow wake and pressure recovery, so mostly skin friction remains
questions.explanation: The dynamic pressure is 540 Pa, so the sphere drag is 5.08 N and the streamlined drag is 0.65 N, a ratio of 7.8. The difference comes from the wake: the tapering tail lets the pressure recover and removes almost all of the pressure drag.
